blogs.title: The Long Shadow of Terror: Reaffirming Deference to the Executive in Enduring Counterterrorism Investigations
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's robust application of judicial deference in *Farahi*, specifically focusing on Exemption 7(A)'s requirement that enforcement proceedings be 'pending or reasonably anticipated.' The article explores how the court navigates the tension between the passage of time—often a fatal flaw in FOIA litigation—and the unique, open-ended nature of counterterrorism investigations involving figures linked to groups like Al Qaeda and the Muslim Brotherhood. It examines Judge Katsas's reasoning that an investigation into potential terror financing and recruitment remains 'ongoing' decades after initial contacts, effectively expanding the temporal scope of 'reasonably anticipated' proceedings in national security contexts.

blogs.title: The Ex Parte Shield: How Sealed Declarations Shape Segregability Analysis in National Security FOIA Cases
blogs.description: Focusing on procedural mechanics, this post dissects the court's handling of ex parte and under-seal declarations in *Farahi*. While FOIA generally favors adversarial testing, this case highlights how courts increasingly rely on private submissions from agencies to resolve complex questions of segregability when public disclosures would defeat the purpose of the exemption. The analysis considers whether the plaintiff's failure to formally oppose the admission of these sealed declarations constitutes a waiver, and discusses the broader implications for transparency when 'meaningful information' is deemed inseparable from classified or sensitive law enforcement data.

blogs.title: 'Interspersed Line-by-Line': Clarifying the High Bar for Reasonable Segregability Under FOIA
blogs.description: This post tackles the often-overlooked doctrine of segregability under 5 U.S.C. § 552(b). Using *Farahi* as a case study, it analyzes why the court rejected Farahi's argument that even tiny fragments of non-exempt text within thousands of pages must be released. The article delves into the precedent set by *Mead Data Central* regarding information that is 'intertwined,' explaining how modern digital records containing dense networks of intelligence make true segregation practically impossible without revealing investigative methods or sources. It argues that *Farahi* reinforces a functional approach to segregability that prioritizes operational security over piecemeal disclosure.
